lessons.title: Fractions and mixed numbers
lessons.summary: Read, simplify and convert proper fractions, improper fractions and mixed numbers for Cambridge IGCSE 0580.
lessons.objective: Read, simplify and convert proper fractions, improper fractions and mixed numbers for Cambridge IGCSE 0580.
lessons.before: Read each example, cover its next step and try the matching question.
lessons.ideas:
In \(\frac{4}{9}\), the denominator \(9\) gives the number of parts in one whole and the numerator \(4\) gives the number counted.

Multiply the numerator and denominator by the same positive whole number. The value is unchanged.

Divide both numbers by a common factor. Once their highest common factor is \(1\), the fraction is in simplest form.
lessons.method:
What do the top and bottom numbers tell you?

In \(\frac{4}{9}\), the denominator \(9\) gives the number of parts in one whole and the numerator \(4\) gives the number counted.

How can two fractions show the same amount?

Multiply the numerator and denominator by the same positive whole number. The value is unchanged.

When has a fraction been simplified completely?

Divide both numbers by a common factor. Once their highest common factor is \(1\), the fraction is in simplest form.
mistakes: Reading the fraction as nine parts out of four swaps the two roles.
Multiplying just one number changes the fraction.
Subtracting the same number from top and bottom does not simplify a fraction.

examples.title: Read the named fraction form
examples.question: Which form is \(\frac{4}{9}\) written in?
examples.solution:
The numerator is \(4\) and the denominator is \(9\).

The numerator is less than the denominator, so it is a proper fraction.

examples.title: Read the named fraction form
examples.question: Which form is \(\frac{13}{6}\) written in?
examples.solution:
The numerator is \(13\) and the denominator is \(6\).

The numerator is greater than the denominator, so it is a improper fraction.

examples.title: Scale both parts of the fraction
examples.question: Find the missing numerator in \(\frac{7}{12}=\frac{n}{36}\).
examples.solution:
The denominator is multiplied by \(3\). To keep the same value, multiply the numerator by that same number.

\(n=7\times3=21\).

lessons.title: Fractions and terminating decimals
lessons.summary: Use place value and exact division to convert terminating decimals and fractions in Cambridge IGCSE 0580.
lessons.objective: Use place value and exact division to convert terminating decimals and fractions in Cambridge IGCSE 0580.
lessons.before: Read each example, cover its next step and try the matching question.
lessons.ideas:
A value with three decimal places can be read as a whole number of thousandths. Write leading or internal zero digits in their original places.

For \(d\) decimal places, write the digits over \(10^d\) and then simplify.

Choose \(10\), \(100\) or another suitable power of ten divisible by the denominator. Scale top and bottom equally.
lessons.method:
How does a decimal tell you the size of the parts?

A value with three decimal places can be read as a whole number of thousandths. Write leading or internal zero digits in their original places.

How do you write a terminating decimal as a fraction?

For \(d\) decimal places, write the digits over \(10^d\) and then simplify.

Can you change the fraction to tenths or hundredths first?

Choose \(10\), \(100\) or another suitable power of ten divisible by the denominator. Scale top and bottom equally.
mistakes: The digit in the thousandths position is just one digit. The complete number may contain many thousandths.
Writing a decimal with three decimal places over \(100\) gives a value ten times too large.
A denominator that looks close to 100 cannot simply be rounded or changed on its own.

examples.title: Locate hundredths and thousandths separately
examples.question: For \(0.378\), give the digit in the hundredths column and the number of thousandths in the whole value.
examples.solution:
To the right of the decimal point the place values are tenths, hundredths and thousandths.

The hundredths digit is \(7\). As the whole value is \(\frac{378}{1000}\), it contains \(378\) thousandths.

examples.title: Locate hundredths and thousandths separately
examples.question: For \(0.049\), give the digit in the hundredths column and the number of thousandths in the whole value.
examples.solution:
To the right of the decimal point the place values are tenths, hundredths and thousandths.

The hundredths digit is \(4\). As the whole value is \(\frac{49}{1000}\), it contains \(49\) thousandths.

examples.title: Use the last decimal place
examples.question: Write \(1.236\) as a fraction in simplest form. Give the numerator and denominator.
examples.solution:
There are \(3\) places after the decimal point. Read the number as \(\frac{1236}{1000}\) using place value.

Divide both parts by their highest common factor, \(4\).

This gives \(\frac{309}{250}\).

lessons.title: Percentages and equivalent forms
lessons.summary: Recognise equivalent fractions, decimals and percentages, including fractional percentages and values above one whole.
lessons.objective: Recognise equivalent fractions, decimals and percentages, including fractional percentages and values above one whole.
lessons.before: Read each example, cover its next step and try the matching question.
lessons.ideas:
\(p\%=\frac p{100}\). One full unit is \(100\%\).

Multiply by \(100\) to get the percentage number, then attach the percent sign.

Divide the percentage number by \(100\) even when it is less than one or greater than one hundred.
lessons.method:
What does the percent sign mean?

\(p\%=\frac p{100}\). One full unit is \(100\%\).

Why multiply the decimal by one hundred?

Multiply by \(100\) to get the percentage number, then attach the percent sign.

What happens with a fractional percentage?

Divide the percentage number by \(100\) even when it is less than one or greater than one hundred.
mistakes: A percentage number can be greater than 100. It then describes more than one whole.
A decimal below \(0.01\) gives a percentage below \(1\%\), not a two-digit percentage.
Dropping the percent sign without dividing changes the value by a factor of 100.

examples.title: Give the same value as a percentage
examples.question: Convert \(\frac{37}{100}\). Give the percentage. Enter the number before the percent sign.
examples.solution:
Divide the numerator by the denominator to give \(0.37\).

Multiply that decimal by \(100\). The fraction equals \(37\%\).

examples.title: Convert between the decimal and percentage
examples.question: Write \(117\%\) as an exact decimal.
examples.solution:
Percent means per hundred. First write the value as \(\frac{117}{100}\).

Dividing by \(100\) gives \(1.17\).

examples.title: Convert between the decimal and percentage
examples.question: Write \(0.054\) as a percentage. Enter the number before the percent sign.
examples.solution:
One whole is \(100\%\). Multiply the decimal value by \(100\).

\(0.054\times100=5.4\) gives \(5.4\%\).

lessons.title: Recurring decimals and fractions (Extended)
lessons.summary: Extended E1.4. Read recurring notation, use the cycle of remainders and convert exactly between recurring decimals and fractions.
lessons.objective: Extended E1.4. Read recurring notation, use the cycle of remainders and convert exactly between recurring decimals and fractions.
lessons.before: Read each example, cover its next step and try the matching question.
lessons.ideas:
A bar covers the full block. One dot marks a single repeated digit. Two dots mark the first and last digits of a longer block.

If the repeat begins immediately, multiply by \(10^n\) for an \(n\)-digit block. The repeating tails line up.

If \(m\) non-recurring digits come first and \(n\) digits repeat, use \(10^{m+n}x\) and \(10^mx\). Subtract when the tails match.
lessons.method:
Which digits recur?

A bar covers the full block. One dot marks a single repeated digit. Two dots mark the first and last digits of a longer block.

Why do powers of ten help?

If the repeat begins immediately, multiply by \(10^n\) for an \(n\)-digit block. The repeating tails line up.

How does a non-recurring prefix change the equation?

If \(m\) non-recurring digits come first and \(n\) digits repeat, use \(10^{m+n}x\) and \(10^mx\). Subtract when the tails match.
mistakes: Putting a mark over a digit before the block changes the value.
Multiplying by 10 may not line up a repeating block of several digits.
The prefix length and the block length do different jobs. Keep zeros inside a block when counting its length.

examples.title: Mark exactly the repeating block
examples.question: Choose the correct bar notation for \(0.1646464\ldots\). The displayed block continues in the same pattern.
examples.solution:
The digits \(1\) come before the block and do not repeat.

The complete block is \(64\). A bar belongs above every digit in that block, giving \(0.1\overline{64}\).

examples.title: Mark exactly the repeating block
examples.question: Choose the correct bar notation for \(2.071071071\ldots\). The displayed block continues in the same pattern.
examples.solution:
The repetition begins immediately after the decimal point.

The complete block is \(071\). A bar belongs above every digit in that block, giving \(2.\overline{071}\).

examples.title: Line up the repeat before subtracting
examples.question: Write \(0.\overline{48}\) as a fraction in simplest form. Give the numerator and denominator.
examples.solution:
The non-recurring block has \(0\) digits and the recurring block has \(2\) digits. Let \(x=0.\overline{48}\).

Shift the two numbers so the same block starts immediately after the decimal point in both rows.

ExpressionValue
\(100x\)\(48.\overline{48}\)
\(1x\)\(0.\overline{48}\)

Subtract the lower row from the upper row. The repeating part cancels, giving \(99x=48\).

Divide by \(99\) and simplify to \(\frac{16}{33}\).
